\chapter{Synthesis --- The Decoder}
\label{ch:synthesis-sound-laws}
\hlchaptermodality{31}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can decode unfamiliar Spanish with three sound laws and three endings.}

Complete ES-C57-sintesis-descifrar: decode hoja and lleno, read a two-ending phrase, and say what a word that resists every rule suggests.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[Practice]{Synthesis — the decoder}

\label{lesson:ES-C57-sintesis-descifrar}



\begin{quote}
Four sound laws and three endings. Before the practice: what do you do with an unfamiliar word starting \emph{h-}? One starting \emph{ll-}? One starting \emph{es-}?
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{what you see} & \textbf{what to try} & \textbf{example} \\
\midrule
\emph{-ch-} & Latin \emph{-ct-} & \emph{noche} $\to$ \textbf{nocturnal} \\
\emph{h-} & put an \emph{f} back & \emph{hijo} $\to$ \textbf{filial} \\
\emph{ll-} & try \emph{cl-}, \emph{pl-}, \emph{fl-} & \emph{llave} $\to$ \textbf{clavicle} \\
\emph{es-} + consonant & take the \emph{e-} off & \emph{escuela} $\to$ \textbf{school} \\
\emph{-ción} & \emph{-tion} & \emph{nación} $\to$ \textbf{nation} \\
\emph{-dad} & \emph{-ty} & \emph{ciudad} $\to$ \textbf{city} \\
\emph{-mente} & \emph{-ly} & \emph{claramente} $\to$ \textbf{clearly} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Seven rules, and between them they will get you through a great deal of written Spanish this book has no room to teach. They also \textbf{stack}: \emph{estación} gives up both ends at once.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: what a decoder is not}]
Be exact about what you have, because overclaiming it will disappoint you at the worst moment. This is a \textbf{reading} tool, and mostly a first-guess one: it will not tell you how to say something, will not give you gender or conjugation, and will sometimes point at the wrong English word.

What it does is remove the feeling that an unfamiliar Spanish word is a wall. Usually it is not — it is a word you already know, wearing clothes you have learned to recognise. That change of expectation is worth more than any word in this chapter: it is what lets you read above your level and get most of it.

\textbf{And when the decoder fails, that is information too.} A word that resists every rule is usually from one of Spanish's non-Latin layers — Arabic, Basque, or the Americas — worth noticing precisely because it breaks a rule you hold.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the seven rules, in order
  \item \textquotedblleft{}hoja, lleno, noche\textquotedblright{} and name the law behind each
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How many rules do you now hold? (\textbf{Seven} — four laws and three endings.) What are they for? (\textbf{Reading}, mostly first guesses.) And what has really changed? (An unfamiliar word is \textbf{no longer a wall}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
